rv.q: The quest for laughs is remorseless, the hilarity near-compulsory.
Overall, this looks like an attempt to emulate Richard Bean’s hit, One Man, Two Guvnors...but ultimately it’s not quite enough to save the enterprise from mediocrity.
Yet for those in need of diverting fluff, it should suit well enough.
Foley’s adaptation is frenzied and farcical without being particularly funny.
Sadly, however, this stage version, rather like the fabled suit, comes apart at the seams.
But the flimsy narrative has nowhere near enough tension to keep one interested.
The staging is inventive, but that and a few nods to fast fashion and a reference to proroguing parliament can't redeem this charmless outfit.
This is a hoot from start to finish.
When Foley’s production commits to the bizarre, as it does here, it’s a winner.
There's an awful lot of frantic activity, but it just careers off the tracks.
But what was a shrewd, surprisingly tender and Academy Award-nominated satire on technology, inventions and social good vs. commercial greed has been turned into a wearingly overplayed farce.
Subtlety and true wit, there is none.

cn.t: This stage adaptation of the Ealing comedy misfires despite committed performances from Stephen Mangan and cast. Critics find Sean Foley's overly broad, slapstick approach strained and unfocused, resulting in labored entertainment that rarely lands its laughs.
